title: Matt Clifford (@matthewclifford)
clean_title: The importance of agency in Britain’s technological future
summary:
This is very thoughtful. Agency is an important and underrated idea in our discourse.
Quoting @KanishkaNarayan
TB: “Put bluntly, the only solution to Britain’s economic weakness is to be found in the application of modern technology more rapidly in British industry.”
The surprise? TB = Tony Benn, addressing the TUC in 1967.
How is it that Benn was asking in 1967 a more modern question than contemporary Westminster still prioritises in 2026?
Through its history, the best of Labour has been not old v new Labour, but hopeful Labour: a sharp focus on weighing up the hopes and fears of our time and of our future, and corralling them into a march of progress.
In recent decades, we lost that focus. As the ground moved under our feet, Westminster's bubble stood still, rehashed debates of the past, defined themselves with loyalties to tribes long extinct, presented failed substance on failed tradmedia, moved our country back. It is painful watching those complicit in that catastrophe still rehashing debates of General Elections past for today. I was 7 at the 1997 GE; so many of us in the PLP just aren’t here to litigate a past we weren't a part of.
The central question for our communities - does Britain get to shape technology, or are we shaped by it? - remained unanswered, indeed unasked. We patronised our communities with the suggestion that technology’s salience was a fixation of techbros, ceding ground to those very techbros.
Our communities, friends and neighbours, meanwhile, puzzled over why their agency, our agency, wasn’t the focus of our politicians.
Why weren’t we spending every hour of every day securing jobs for our kids’ and their kids’ future, a question unanswerable without reference to a plan to shape the next wave of technology?
Why did no child in our country see a company go from zero to top 10, where 8 in 10 did in the US, driving our big wedge in prosperity, taxes to undo austerity’s damage, and influence between our countries, another question with answers rooted in technology?
Why did millions of our sick neighbours spend a million moments filling arcane DWP forms, treated with inhumanity, waiting weeks for life-saving money, left to an exploding digital subprime consumer credit market and a daily 8am grind of GP and CAMHS queues, whilst frontier technology enabled their healthy neighbours a life of ever more instant payment and provision?
Why did a maternity care doctor say to me the only moment of recent relief, a return to the original promise of her vocation in medicine, was her experience of AI transcription that let her focus on care?
Why wasn’t Britain genuinely moving the needle again on the climate crisis by shaping technologies that could do what global innovation in solar PV and wind turbines did?
Why weren’t we securing Britain’s agency in the defining national security race of our age, our ability to wield AI drones and counter drone defence systems?
Why wasn’t our politics quicker and surer to support the agency of families, of children, women and girls, of minority groups, indeed of British democracy, as we faced the nation-tearing onslaught of bot farms?
These are fundamentally future Labour questions, deserving our obsession and the most hopeful Labour answers. Those answers do not lie in old or new Labour. The axes of those divides - more technology or less technology, more regulation or less regulation, state monopoly or private monopoly, state control or individual discretion, zero US tech or only US tech - are obviously not even the right questions. Even in Tony Blair’s telling, they invert his original promise: obsessing with radical means for shrunken ends, not the radical ends of securing British agency, underpinned by clear-eyed realism of means.
Quietly, as far as an uninterested Westminster bubble is concerned, we have started to rebuild an agenda focused on the most radical of goals for British AI: restoring the agency of British families, British entrepreneurs and the British state, answering the three questions that determine our future.
▪️First, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐬. At the site of an old car manufacturing plant, hundreds of jobs coming after a decade of nothing. At an old steelworks, the biggest capital investment in decades, nearly half a billion on community investment alone. At a third site, the dated promise of clean energy only feasible now with the pull of major AI investment. At the proud site of the UK’s largest listed tech firm, billions more in investment, and the most gripping stories of apprentices leaving hairdressing to shape the future of AI. The agency of a family able to choose both ambition of work and affection for home. Similar agency in the most far-reaching government in its toughness against social media: standing up to the richest man in the world, staring him down, pioneering global change, securing the dignity of women and girls across our country. On children’s safety, the deepest agency for families and young people to shape our future: find me another policy area where over a hundred thousand have had their direct say, where mums have taken hour-long buses and young teens minibuses in every nation and region to share their pains, to ask their tough questions, to experience the collective agency of shaping a safer future.
▪️Second, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐫𝐬. The last wave of technology concentrated in too few places, enriching too few people. So, we have blown open the doors for worker prosperity: Britain now has the world’s best support for workers’ ownership of shares in startups. Billions more to British entrepreneurs from the British Business Bank. Millions in procurement buying British AI: big contracts like that for Quantexa, small rapid contracts for startups via Sovereign AI. And even more worker support on way, as we consult on changes to non-competes holding workers back from switching jobs.
▪️Third, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞. A remarkable revolution in state capacity is being celebrated internationally. AISI has outcompeted frontier labs’ billions with public mission, uniquely assuring British security from modern threats. Researcher after researcher tells me how ARIA has rescued them from the modern oppression of poor bureaucracy. Sovereign AI, though early, has already built an industrial policy path that has compelled the world’s best firms - Isomorphic, Ineffable - to pick UK government as its only UK investor. Where Callaghan funded Inmos, spawning Wales’ compound semiconductor cluster and our national champion ARM, we are renewing that hopeful Labour promise for today with our AI hardware focus. All efforts celebrated internationally (NYT just this week), making Britain the standout best in Europe for AI, putting billions into our economy, creating jobs in every corner of our country, millions in taxes ahead, a boost to national security today. As so many say, the agency of the state is the spark that lights up our national culture of agency well beyond the state; it is a spark so palpable in UK AI today.
What could be more Labour? Radical goals - control back in the hands of British families, restoration of linked risk and reward for entrepreneurs and workers, proud state capacity - being delivered with relentless energy.

Agency is a crucial but often overlooked idea in our discourse, especially regarding how Britain interacts with technology. title: Matt Clifford (@matthewclifford)
clean_title: Thoughts on the UK’s sovereign AI strategy and building in the UK
summary:
Ross is a smart guy who knows what he’s talking about. This is worth a read.
Quoting @rosstaylor90
A few words on the Sovereign AI debate, having built several LLMs in Meta while in the UK and now working as a UK based startup:
1. Lots of people are trying to do the right thing to make the UK a better place to start AI companies. Time lags until the benefit show, but you should judge on the intent now. I support the direction of travel!
2. DeepMind has been enormously beneficial for the UK, but it has muddied the waters for a sovereign LLM company to emerge as (until recently) the Government continued to celebrate it as a British achievement / push it as a national champion.
3. Similarly, people are now celebrating recent US investment in King’s Cross, while also wanting more UK sovereignty. Clearly some income effects here, but I would worry about the substitution effects too. AI is not like other types of foreign investment.
4. The relevant talent nexuses in UK that could develop a competitive foundation model are from GDM and old Meta AI GenAI. Also some folks from smaller groups, ex Conjecture, Stability. The talent is still there, although a lot was snapped up by US FM companies in the past year. I personally think it’s not too difficult to develop new talent either from UK universities, but you probably need an ex GDM or Meta core (Gemini or Llama). Or if not: show evidence first (technical reports) before claiming you can do it.
5. Building an LLM is very different from doing regular AI research - skillset is different. Former is closer to engineering; long hours, often unsexy work. Important to distinguish between these two types of talent in the UK ecosystem; arguably too much focus on the latter / ideas guys.
6. On research - DeepSeek R1 post-train cost $300k . Yes, they also needed an ablation budget and to train a base model, invest in infra and talent - and yes the cost of an R1 moment is increasing year on year - but the idea that you need $1bn plus immediately to show results is complete FUD. You need billions to scale, not to validate new directions.
7. In my experience, every failed LLM effort (from model results perspective) I witnessed in the past came from a combination of poor leadership, politics, unclear vision, and premature scaling. Good efforts usually started from small teams who had worked with each other for a long time, had shared thesis, and scaled progressively in bite-sized pieces. Some recent lessons here for neolabs as well.
8. Things take time. Eg we’ve spent ~12 months mostly on internal infra just to get into the position to be able to make big swings. It’s important to nurture new companies through the initial phase. Expectation management is also crucial. I think expecting new UK companies to have single big bang releases is very dangerous; sort of like overwatering a plant. The correct release pattern is “decent”. “decent”, “decent”, “quite good actually”, “holy shit”.
9. Please don’t allow politicians or journalists to kill recent or upcoming AI investment efforts. We will need way more - at the price of potential inefficiency in places - as AI is existential for the country. Ambitious projects are usually incredibly fragile in the early stages; look after them!
10. Mythos is a good triggering moment, but what’s coming will make it look like a toy, so it’s worth building for what’s coming in 5 years time - not a current generation model.
Very proud to be building in the UK - more to share on that soon - alongside many other great early stage AI companies! 🇬🇧
clean_summary:
Ross, a knowledgeable figure in AI, shares insights on the UK’s efforts to develop sovereign large language models (LLMs). He emphasizes that while many are working to improve the environment for AI startups, the benefits may take time to materialize, and the intent behind policies is what matters most.

He notes that DeepMind has been beneficial for the UK but has complicated the emergence of a sovereign LLM company due to its status as a national champion. The debate around foreign investment, especially US funding in UK projects, highlights concerns about sovereignty and talent retention. The UK has talent from groups like GDM, Meta AI, and smaller startups, though much has been absorbed by US firms. Developing new talent from UK universities is feasible, especially with experience from companies like GDM or Meta.

Building an LLM requires a different skill set than traditional AI research—more engineering-focused, involving long hours and practical work. Cost-wise, efforts like DeepSeek’s R1 model show that scaling costs are rising, but immediate results can be achieved without billion-dollar budgets. Failures often stem from poor leadership, politics, unclear vision, and premature scaling, while successful projects start small, scale gradually, and have cohesive teams.

Ross stresses that building in AI takes time, with months spent on infrastructure before making significant progress. Supporting early-stage companies and managing expectations is crucial, as big releases are rare early on. Politicians and journalists should be cautious not to undermine AI investments, which are vital for the country’s future. He believes that the coming advancements will surpass current models significantly, making it worthwhile to build for the future rather than current capabilities.

He concludes with pride in building in the UK and hints at sharing more about his work soon, celebrating the many early-stage AI companies in the country.

Today we're launching Intercept: a $500M philanthropic initiative to make respiratory infections, like the common cold and flu, a thing of the past.
We treat respiratory infections as a minor nuisance, but that’s really not the case. Most of us will spend 5% of our lives (!) sick from these viruses, they kill 1M people a year, cost $600B annually in productivity, and periodically threaten civilization through pandemics.
So, if they’re such a big problem, why haven’t we dealt with them yet? Last year we convened ~40 leading scientists, pharma R&D leaders, biotech investors, and regulatory experts to better understand that.
We heard two main reasons:
(1) First, it’s just technically very challenging: respiratory viruses represent hundreds of distinct, mutating strains across several families. Fortunately, recent breakthroughs make this newly possible.
(2) Second is a lack of funding: broad-spectrum solutions have historically been underfunded, in part because they’re not a great fit for most philanthropic or commercial funding (and while COVID generated a burst of activity around preventing and understanding respiratory infections through an influx of new funding, that hasn't been sustained).
We think that with enough focus and funding, this might be solvable. Intercept is a $500 million philanthropic initiative that will take advantage of new tools to catalyze the development and deployment of two types of products: broad-spectrum preventatives and air cleaning technologies.
This problem is undoubtedly difficult. But it’s more tractable now than it’s ever been. We think we should give it our best shot.
We’re enormously grateful to our anchor funders: @stripe, @AnthropicAI, @TheFluLab, @FoundationOAI and individuals from Jane Street.
And, I’m very excited to be building this with @incredutility and the rest of the team.

Respiratory viruses cause significant health and economic burdens, killing a million people annually and costing $600 billion in productivity each year. Despite their impact, tackling these viruses has been difficult due to their diversity and mutation, as well as underfunding of broad-spectrum solutions. Recent scientific breakthroughs and increased funding could now make it possible to develop broad-spectrum preventatives and air cleaning technologies. The initiative is supported by major funders including Stripe, AnthropicAI, The Flu Lab, and Foundation OAI, with the goal of accelerating progress in this challenging area.

clean_title: UK startup uses AI to develop and market first molecule
summary:
A UK startup is set to be the FIRST EVER to get an AI-designed molecule into market!
The CEO (@jgodwin_ai) is an ex-DeepMind researcher who is now using AI to discover exotic new materials.
The first material they've produced is a cooling fluid designed to prevent next-generation GPUs from overheating.
They've done this using Orb - their AI model for simulating the quantum mechanical behaviour of atoms, which is the only model that can simulate 100,000 atoms on a single GPU.
It runs ten times faster than the nearest alternative — outperforming models from Microsoft, Meta and leading academic labs.
Earlier this year the company (@Orbital_Ind) raised $50m from @pluralplatform (@soundboy) to go even further.
There's a lot of talk about how strong AI is in London. This is a clear example where a UK team and company is truly building world-leading frontier AI.
VERY COOL - congrats @gin_james @Dmiodovnik
